title: Listen Carefully

clips.speaker: narrator
clips.text: He was not mad, the old man's housemate insisted. Only nervous. His illness had sharpened his senses, especially his hearing. He heard everything in heaven and earth. Surely that proved he was sane. His listener should judge how calmly he told the story. He loved the old man, who had never hurt him. He wanted no money. But that pale blue eye, covered by a thin film like a vulture's, made his blood turn cold. He would kill the old man and close it forever. For seven nights, at midnight, he eased open the bedroom door. Slowly, he slipped his head inside with a covered lantern. He let one thin ray fall across the eye. Always closed. He could do nothing. He hated the eye, not the man. Each morning, he greeted his housemate warmly.

clips.speaker: narrator
clips.text: On the eighth night, his thumb slipped on the lantern's metal fastening.

clips.speaker: narrator
clips.text: the old man cried. For an hour, he stood perfectly still while the old man sat upright, listening. From the bed came a small groan of terror. At last, he opened the lantern a little. The narrow beam struck the eye. Wide open. Then he heard it: a low, quick beating, like a watch wrapped in cotton. The old man's heart. Faster it beat, and louder. What if a neighbour heard? He rushed forward with a yell. The old man shrieked once. He dragged him to the floor and pulled the heavy bed over him. For a while, the beating continued. Then silence. He hid the body beneath three floorboards and carefully fitted them back. No mark remained.

clips.speaker: narrator
clips.text: At four in the morning came a knock. Three police officers stood outside; a neighbour had heard a shriek. He smiled and welcomed them. The cry had been his own, he explained—a bad dream. The old man was away in the country. He showed them the house, then brought chairs into the bedroom. Calm and confident, he sat directly above the hidden body. The officers settled down and chatted. A ringing troubled his ears. He spoke louder, but now the sound was clear: low, quick, like a watch wrapped in cotton.

clips.speaker: narrator
clips.text: He stood and paced. He scraped his chair across the boards. Still the beating grew louder. The officers kept smiling and talking. They seemed to hear nothing. But they knew. They must know. Their pleasant smiles were mocking him. How could they sit there? How could he bear another second? "Stop pretending!" he screamed. "I did it! Tear up the planks! Here, beneath my feet! It is the beating of his hideous heart!"
